title: The latency trap of slower backing stores
text: Hi, I'm Ash. Imagine an application serving millions of requests, sessions, product lookups, counters, rate limits, real-time data. If every request depends on a slower storage path, latency can climb quickly as traffic grows. Ries changes that path. It keeps data in memory, processes requests efficiently, and can distribute the key space across multiple nodes. So, how does that architecture stay fast when the request count explodes? title: Scalability bottlenecks: Hot keys, memory limits, and eviction policies
text: Network traffic, and command processing across the cluster. RED's cluster makes that distribution predictable with hash slots. The key space is divided into 16,384 slots. A key is hashed to one of those slots and each slot belongs to a particular primary node. A clusteraware client can use that mapping to send a command directly to the node responsible for its key. Different slot ranges can then be spread across different machines. There's another bottleneck that has nothing to do with finding a key in memory. The network round trip. Normally a client can send one command, wait for its response, send the next command, and wait again. Do that thousands of times and network latency adds up. Ry's pipelining lets the client send multiple commands without waiting for every individual response first. Resiz processes the commands and returns the

Replies, reducing repeated round trips and increasing the amount of useful work done per unit of time. In code, the client creates a pipeline, cue several commands, then executes them together. The important point is not that the commands become one giant Ry's operation. The advantage is that the client does not wait for a complete network round trip between every command. In production, pipelines should still be reasonably bounded because Rudy's has to cue replies until the client reads them. Now imagine the cluster topology changes. A slot may move to another node or a failover may change which node serves a range of slots. If a client sends a command to the wrong node, Ry's cluster can return a moved redirection pointing to the node that currently owns that slot. Clusteraware clients update their routing information. So normal requests

Can again go directly to the appropriate node. Sharding increases capacity, but what happens when a primary fails? Ry's cluster can keep replicas of primary nodes on other machines. If a primary becomes unavailable and the cluster can perform a failover, an eligible replica can be promoted to serve that primary hash slots. Replication improves availability, but it should not be confused with a guarantee of zero data loss. Ry's cluster replication is a synchronous, so failure timing and configuration still matter. Put it together and there is no single millions of requests switch. Keeping the working data in memory makes common operations fast. Event-driven networking handles many client connections efficiently. Pipelining reduces repeated network round trips. Hash slots divide the key space and RD's cluster spreads those slots across nodes. Replicas provide failover options. Together, those mechanisms let a RD's

Deployment distribute both the data and the request load as traffic grows. Limits still exist. A hotkey can concentrate traffic on one node even when the rest of the cluster has capacity. Large values or expensive commands can increase latency. Memory is finite, so data set size, expiration, and eviction policy matter. Network round trips, payload sizes, persistence, and client behavior matter too. Ries can be extremely fast, but scaling still requires understanding the workload instead of assuming memory makes every operation free. The mental model is simple. Ry's keeps the hot data path fast in memory, handles client traffic efficiently, uses pipelining to reduce network overhead, and uses hash slots to spread data across cluster nodes when one machine isn't enough. Replicas add failover options. That's how riddies can be designed to serve request heavy applications at very large scale.
